To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the growth response of post smolting salmon to the environment is an important determinant of survival and recruitment and (ii) the mechanism of growth-mediated survival and recruitment involves the interaction of salmon with the foodweb, which in turn is affected by climate forcing, and that this mechanism is most apparent in the first summer at sea.

1. SST and the Atlantic Multidecadals Oscillation (AMO) are negatively correlated with postsmolt survival and recruitment; 2. The postsmolt nursery region is in the North Atlantic, where SST and the AMO are negatively correlated with salmon survival; 3. Postsmolt growth is positively correlated with post smolts survival and recruitment.

(1) the growth of European Atlantic salmon post smolts is negatively related to sea surface temperature during summer, (2) the growth of postsmolts is positively related to the abundance of pelagic prey and negatively related to the abundance and size of predators, and (3) post smolt growth is positively related to post smolt survival, which is negatively related to salmon recruitment
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms controlling recruitment of Atlantic salmon, S. salar, to the adult stage in the sea.
the mechanisms of salmon recruitment and the role of climate forcing in controlling salmon recruitment.
understanding how climate change affects the marine ecology of salmon, and how this knowledge can be used to improve the management of salmon stocks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mechanism of salmon recruitment is the interaction of postsmolt and predator populations, with climate forcing acting through SST and forage availability.
the decline in European salmon recruitment is due to a combination of increased SST and reduced forage, which results in poor post smolt growth and survival, and hence reduced recruitment.
climate forcing, through its effects on SST and forage, has resulted in a multidecadally declining European Atlantic salmon stock complex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
European Atlantic salmon recruitment is controlled by the interaction between physical forcing, biological responses, and growth.
the recruitment success of European Atlantic salmon is determined by a suite of environmental factors that affect the post smolt period.

climate change has affected the European Atlantic salmon stock complex through a reduction in postsmolt survival, and that this has occurred via the growth response of post smolting salmon to a change in the marine environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
climate change and its impact on the physical environment, the foodweb, and the growth of postsmolts may be the main drivers of European Atlantic salmon recruitment.

salmon recruitment appears to have a strong link to climate and food web dynamics in the North Sea and adjacent waters, and that the link to SST is likely to be mediated by the growth of postsmolt Atlantic salmon.

the decline in European salmon recruitment appears to have been driven by a combination of climate and foodweb change, and that the decline is not a result of a change in the marine survival of adults.
